title: Quebecor CEO defends Telus bid, cites falling wireless prices and Canada's sovereignty

image.caption: Quebecor president and CEO Pierre Karl Péladeau waits to speak at the Freedom Mobile Arch concert venue in Vancouver on June 5. (Darryl Dyck/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New

Quebecor CEO Pierre Karl Péladeau is defending his company's $31-billion bid to buy Telus amid concerns over competition in Canada's telecom sector, arguing the cost of wireless plans is dropping and non-Canadian companies are trying to expand.
Montreal-based telecom has submitted $31-billion proposal for Telus to review
· CBC News
· Posted: Nov 22, 2026 4:00 AM EST | Last Updated: 31 minutes ago

Quebecor Inc. CEO Pierre Karl Péladeau is defending his company's $31-billion bid to buy Telus Corp. amid concerns over competition in Canada's telecom sector, arguing the cost of wireless plans is dropping and non-Canadian companies are trying to expand.

"Telecom assets are strategic for our country — we all know this. And then therefore, we need to make sure that we're going to be on the same footing," Péladeau said in an interview on Rosemary Barton Live airing Sunday morning.

The Montreal-based telecom, media and entertainment company said on Monday that it submitted a non-binding proposal to Telus in June to serve as a basis for negotiations and that the Vancouver-based corporation is currently reviewing an enhanced proposal submitted by Quebecor earlier this month.

Quebecor's move comes three years after the federal government approved Rogers Communications' acquisition of Shaw Communications on the condition that Freedom Mobile be sold to Quebecor to preserve a four-player market.

Péladeau told CBC chief political correspondent Rosemary Barton that his company has been servicing Freedom Mobile and the Canadian market "pretty efficiently, and our results talk by themselves. We look forward to being able to continue to do the same with the Telus assets."
Quebecor's $31B bid to buy Telus: What it means for your phone bill
Asked how a merger of this size would help with Canadians' wireless costs, Péladeau said prices continue to fall after his company acquired Freedom Mobile.
"Our earnings are growing, our free cash flow is growing," he said. "Why would you change a successful strategy?"

According to Canada's annual telecom report, consumer prices for cellular services declined in recent years but ticked back up in 2025. Canada still had some of the highest wireless prices compared with other developed countries.

items: If Quebecor buys Telus, less competition could mean higher cellphone bills, experts say

blocks.text: Quebecor is currently Canada's fourth-largest telecom company. With its $14.77-billion market capitalization and Telus's $21.72-billion market cap, the potential deal would make Quebecor larger than Rogers or Bell by that metric.

Péladeau also framed the proposed bid as a way of protecting Canada's sovereignty, noting Elon Musk's satellite internet provider Starlink services parts of the Canadian market and is likely hungry to expand its operations.

"[Starlink's] business model is the world, like Netflix's business model was the world," Péladeau said, adding that Netflix "destroyed a Canadian industry" despite not having a licence with the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission (CRTC).
Quebecor is currently Canada's fourth-largest telecom company, with a $14.77-billion market capitalization. (Christopher Katsarov/The Canadian Press)

Telus says it has formed a special committee to review the offer and determine the value of the potential deal. So far, the committee has discovered a number of "significant risks," John Manley, the chair of Telus's board of directors, said in a statement on Monday issued by the company.
Telus also takes issue with how the Quebecor proposal values the company.
Manley said Telus would continue to engage with Quebecor, the government and regulatory authorities about those concerns while exploring alternatives.
The federal perspective so far

In its news release on Monday, Quebecor acknowledged that Canada's Competition Bureau — along with other authorities, such as the CRTC and Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada — will need to approve the deal.
Earlier this week, Prime Minister Mark Carney said more competition, lower prices and better service would be key to any decision regarding the telecom sector.
'This is the last thing we need': NDP asks feds to block Quebecor's Telus bid

Carney declined to comment directly on Quebecor's proposal but said that under certain circumstances and depending on the market structure, an oligopoly situation can lead to more competition with fewer players. He didn't elaborate further.
Péladeau said he doesn't think anyone would disagree with Carney's comments, noting that even if there are three Canadian companies, there will still be other competition, like Starlink.
On Friday, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said his party has not yet seen the proposal but would study it and base its judgment on the principle of lowering prices for consumers.

items: Why Quebecor wants to buy Telus and what it could mean for British Columbians

blocks.text: Poilievre also criticized Carney's comments, saying he has never seen "any economist anywhere in the world say that oligarchies ultimately bring prices down.... Once again, Mr. Carney favours the corporate power brokers over the consumers."
NDP Leader Avi Lewis has called on the Competition Bureau to cancel the sale, saying it will increase costs for consumers and trigger layoffs.

"We already pay some of the highest cellphone prices in the world," he said. "I just think it's so obvious to the vast majority of people who are suffering under this cost-of-living crisis that this is just yet another thing where the big boys just ... swallow up another company."
